questions.scenario: Kestrel Care's HR team has drafted a short guideline for managers: Claude may be used to draft job descriptions, interview questions and offer letters. Managers now ask about two further uses — helping decide which candidates to interview, and writing a short performance-improvement conversation plan for an employee who has already been told their performance is unsatisfactory.
questions.stem: Which TWO uses fit the guideline as drafted? Choose TWO.

options.text: Drafting the interview questions for a role, because the questions describe the job rather than judge a person.
Producing a performance-improvement conversation plan for an employee already in a live process, because the plan's content comes from the manager.
Drafting the job description for a newly approved role, because no existing employee is affected.
Writing an internal newsletter summarising that the guideline now exists, since announcing policy is not using the tool.

questions.explanation: The guideline as drafted permits **drafting documents about a role** — job descriptions and interview questions describe the job, not the people. It does not extend to anything touching a person's position, and a performance-improvement plan sits squarely in a live process affecting one employee, whatever the content came from. Announcing a policy is not a use of the tool at all.

whyWrong.B: This is advice about a named employee's future, inside a process they are already in. Drafting is drafting whether the words come from the manager or not; the guideline does not cover it.
whyWrong.D: Writing a newsletter about the guideline is not an application of the tool to the work the guideline governs, so it neither needs nor demonstrates permission. It also should not be drafted with Claude if the guideline is silent on communication of that kind.

questions.mindset: Drafting documents about a job is different from producing anything that affects a person's position.

questions.scenario: A council's planning department receives about 60 objections to a proposed development each month. Each objection must be summarised and mapped to the material consideration it relates to. The planning officer wants to send the full objection letters, including the objectors' names, addresses and the content of their medical circumstances where raised.
questions.stem: What is the MOST defensible position for the department?

options.text: The letters are already public documents submitted to the council, so there is no confidentiality consideration and the tool can be used as proposed.

Use Claude to summarise the objections, but not on documents that identify the objector: remove names, addresses and health content, and keep the mapping to material considerations. The human planning officer remains the decision-maker on whether an objection is relevant.
Use Claude on the letters as submitted, because the decision about which objections count is ultimately a matter of judgement rather than a matter of fact.
Decline to use Claude for this work entirely, since anything touching public planning decisions is outside the tool's permitted uses.

questions.explanation: The material considerations are a matter of **public judgement, not pattern-finding** — but the reading and summarising work is exactly the kind of high-volume text task the tool is good at. The defensible line separates them: strip the identifying and health content before the document goes anywhere, keep the summarising, and leave the judgement call about an objection's relevance with the planning officer. Public availability of a document is not a reason to include identity and health data in an assistant.

whyWrong.A: That argument conflates two different things: the objection being a public document and the objector being an identifiable person who raised health circumstances. The first permits disclosure; it does not make the second appropriate to process.
whyWrong.C: The judgement argument describes a different task. Deciding which objections count is exactly the part that should not be delegated, and it says nothing about whether the identifying content should be sent.
whyWrong.D: Summarising submitted documents is a routine reading task. Refusing it wholesale removes a legitimate use and leaves the department doing sixty summaries a month by hand.

questions.mindset: Separate the mechanical work you can delegate from the judgement you must keep, and strip identity before anything is sent.

questions.scenario: An insurance claims officer asks Claude to help triage incoming claims into three queues: straightforward, needs investigation, needs a senior assessor. She has been told by a colleague that the tool 'will make the calls for you'. The insurer's policy is silent on triage.
questions.stem: What is the BEST response from the officer's manager?

options.text: Approve the proposal, since triage is a low-stakes classification task and the policy has not prohibited it.

Treat it as a case needing a decision before use: ask the insurer's named owner for AI use to rule on claim triage, and in the meantime use the tool only to summarise each claim, leaving the queue assignment to a person.
Refuse it, because anything that affects the handling of a customer's claim is outside permitted use.
Approve it as a pilot for one month with the officer making the final call, and revisit if no problems appear.

questions.explanation: Silence is not permission, and this is not a neutral classification: which queue a claim lands in determines delay, investigation and who handles a customer's case. Where policy has no answer, the route is to the **named owner of AI use** — not a local approval. Keeping summarising while a person assigns the queue is a proportionate interim position that delivers the volume benefit without delegating the consequential decision.

whyWrong.A: The absence of a prohibition is the argument, not the justification. Claim handling affects customers and is the kind of use an insurer would expect its AI owner to have ruled on.
whyWrong.C: A blanket refusal is disproportionate. Summarising claims is a legitimate reading task, and the question is where the decision sits, not whether the tool may be involved at all.
whyWrong.D: A month-long pilot of a use nobody has ruled on creates a de facto decision by inaction, and 'no problems appeared' over a month is weak evidence for a consequential workflow.

questions.mindset: When policy is silent on something consequential, get the named owner's ruling rather than making the call locally.

questions.scenario: A secondary-school teacher has 140 history essays to mark before report cards are due in nine days. She wants to give each essay to Claude with the student's name and grade attached and a request to assign a mark and a comment, then adjust the results herself afterwards.
questions.stem: What is the MOST appropriate position?

options.text: Approve it with the adjustment step, since the teacher retains final responsibility for every mark awarded.

Decline the use of the tool for assigning marks or grades to named students. If she wants help with writing, a marked exemplar with the student's name removed can be used to develop comment wording, with the teacher's own judgement applied to each student.
Approve it for students who have already received a provisional mark, since those cases involve less risk.
Approve it provided that the essays are anonymised, since anonymisation removes the concern entirely.

questions.explanation: Assigning a mark to a named student is a **consequential judgement about a child**, and a review step afterwards does not change what is being asked of the model — it is the judgement itself. The alternative is genuinely useful and avoids the problem entirely: an anonymised exemplar with the teacher's own marks and comments shows exactly the standard being written to, so the tool helps with the writing while the judgement stays with the teacher. Anonymisation reduces the data problem; it does not address the assessment question.

whyWrong.A: Retaining final responsibility is true of many uses and is not what makes them appropriate. Here the question is whether the judgement should be sought from the model at all, and a review of 140 marks under deadline pressure will not be a real check.
whyWrong.C: A provisional mark is still a mark on a named child's record, and creating a two-track situation where some marks came from a different process is its own fairness problem.
whyWrong.D: Anonymising the essays is a good data-minimisation step and does not change that the model is being asked to grade children. It addresses the second problem and leaves the first.

questions.mindset: Final human responsibility does not make a consequential judgement delegable — anonymise for privacy, but do not outsource the judgement.

questions.scenario: Torrington Water's communications team drafts about 40 notices a year about supply interruptions. Their template is fixed, the facts come from an operations log, and every notice is checked by the duty manager before it goes out. A new employee has asked whether Claude could produce the first draft of each notice from the log entry.
questions.stem: What is the MOST accurate assessment?

options.text: This is a strong candidate for use: repetitive, template-bound work from a factual source, with a named human accountable for every notice before it is sent.
This is appropriate only if the notices are re-read by legal first, because they are public communications about a service failure.
This is not appropriate, because anything a customer reads must be written by a member of staff.
This is appropriate as long as the model is set to its most capable setting, because public notices must not contain mistakes.

questions.explanation: The features of an appropriate use line up unusually well here: the work is **repetitive**, the **output shape is fixed**, the **input is a factual operational record** rather than an opinion or a judgement about a person, and a **named person is accountable** for the notice before it reaches anyone. There is no assessment of individuals and no discretion being delegated. The duty-manager check is not a formality here — it is what makes the use defensible.

whyWrong.B: Legal review of forty template-bound service notices is disproportionate and is not what the risk profile calls for. The material facts are the interruption details and the published template.
whyWrong.C: It is a claim about authorship, not about appropriateness. Plenty of appropriate drafting work is AI-assisted, and the question is who is accountable for the result, not who typed it.
whyWrong.D: Model capability does not change the governance question, and a capable model still needs the human check that this process already has. Setting the most capable tier for forty routine drafts is also a cost and speed mistake.

questions.mindset: Appropriate use is repetitive, template-bound work from facts, with a named person accountable before it reaches anyone.

questions.scenario: A marketing coordinator wants to test how Claude summarises customer feedback so the team can prioritise a backlog. She exports the last 400 tickets from the helpdesk. The export contains customer names, email addresses, order numbers, and in about 30 cases a free-text description of a health-related complaint.
questions.stem: Which TWO actions are MOST appropriate before she proceeds? Choose TWO.

options.text: Classify the export before sending anything: names and contact details are identifying, order numbers are pseudonymous but linkable, and free-text health content is sensitive regardless of whose name is attached.
Confirm the policy and the approved data route for this organisation before uploading, since the presence of sensitive free text means the handling question comes first.
Strip the email addresses only, because names in a customer support export are necessary for follow-up.
Ask a colleague to try the same export in a personal Claude account first, to see whether the summary looks useful before involving the company's systems.

questions.explanation: Two steps, in this order. **Classify the material before it leaves** — name and email identify, order number links back to a person, and free-text health content is sensitive in its own right, so removing the email does not make the export safe. And confirm the **approved route and policy**, because once sensitive content is in a personal account it is already outside the organisation's control, which is why the colleague's shortcut is the wrong order.

whyWrong.C: Names are the most direct identifier in the file, not the least important one, and the health-related free text remains in the export regardless of what is removed from the name column.
whyWrong.D: Testing on a personal account first creates exactly the exposure the classification step is meant to avoid: sensitive content now sits in a system the organisation does not govern and cannot clean up.

questions.mindset: Classify the material and confirm the approved route before uploading anything — removing one identifier does not declassify the rest.

questions.scenario: A support lead wants to give Claude 60 anonymised support transcripts to find recurring themes. The anonymisation script replaced names and order numbers, but left ages, postcodes, employer names and the exact wording of each customer's complaint — including, in nine cases, a description of an ongoing health condition.
questions.stem: What is the BEST assessment?

options.text: The file is acceptable because names and order numbers are gone, and that is the standard the policy requires.

The file is not yet acceptable. Age plus postcode plus employer is re-identifying in a small population, and the retained health descriptions are sensitive content that anonymising identity does not address.
The file is acceptable if the analysis is only used to write the summary internally and is never quoted, since the point of the policy is to prevent external disclosure.
The file should be deleted rather than improved, because customer complaint transcripts are never suitable for any internal analysis.

questions.explanation: Anonymisation has been applied at the level of the **obvious identifiers** and stopped there. Age plus postcode plus employer is a combination that re-identifies people in small populations, and the health descriptions are sensitive content whose sensitivity survives the removal of names. The remedy is to broaden the anonymisation to quasi-identifiers and to handle the health content under the right policy, not to abandon the analysis.

whyWrong.A: This assumes the redaction script achieved what 'anonymised' means. Removing direct identifiers is the easy half; quasi-identifiers and sensitive content are what the word is meant to cover.
whyWrong.C: Internal-only use is still processing sensitive material in a system outside the original boundary. Purpose does not change the classification of the content.
whyWrong.D: This is over-correction. Complaint analysis is a legitimate use; the problem is the breadth of the redaction and the presence of health content, both of which are fixable.

questions.mindset: Anonymisation means removing quasi-identifiers and sensitive content, not just names and reference numbers.

questions.scenario: A law firm's policy says client material may be processed with company AI tools where the client's engagement letter permits it. A partner asks a paralegal to run a batch of client documents through Claude to find a pattern in disputed amounts. The file contains 40 different clients' documents. She checks and finds engagement letters for 12 of them; the rest are silent.
questions.stem: Which TWO actions should the paralegal take? Choose TWO.

options.text: Proceed with the 12 clients whose engagement letters permit it, and hold back the other 28 until their position is established.
Look at the remaining 28 engagement letters directly, because older template wording may simply be silent rather than a refusal.
Proceed with all 40, since the instruction comes from a partner and the firm's own policy is what matters.
Remove the client names from the documents and proceed with all 40, since the analysis concerns disputed amounts rather than identity.

questions.explanation: The policy's condition is explicit: **permitted by the engagement letter**, which is a per-client permission, not a firm-wide one. Twelve clients have given it, so that work can proceed. For the other 28 the right step is to read the letters themselves rather than assume — silence in an older template may be a drafting gap rather than a refusal, and checking costs minutes. What is not available is treating a partner's instruction as a permission the client has not given, or treating de-identification as a substitute for consent.

whyWrong.C: A partner's instruction does not supply a permission the client has not given. The firm's own policy is precisely what requires the engagement letter, so this reading contradicts the rule being invoked.
whyWrong.D: De-identification is about identification, not consent. The engagement letters are silent for 28 clients whatever the file contains, and anonymised material can still be confidential material.

questions.mindset: Per-client permission means per-client checking — read the letters that are silent, and treat silence as unresolved rather than as consent.

questions.scenario: An operations manager receives an anonymous employee survey with 900 free-text comments. About 40 comments can be identified by their content — a named project, an unusual role, a small team. He wants Claude to produce a theme report for the board.
questions.stem: What is the BEST way to handle this?

options.text: Use it as it is, since the platform guarantees anonymity and the comments carry no names.

Check with the survey owner whether the identifiable comments were expected, and either suppress them or aggregate them into a form that cannot be traced back to an individual before any use of the material.
Exclude the 40 identifiable comments and proceed, without raising it, since that is the simplest defensible option.
Proceed only after removing any comment that mentions a specific team, project or role, since those are the identifiers involved.

questions.explanation: The comments are **pseudonymised, not anonymous**, and in a small organisation an identifiable comment about a named project is re-identifying to everyone who was there. The right step is to establish whether this was anticipated by the survey owner — because if it was not, that is a finding in its own right — and to suppress or aggregate those comments before the material is used. Suppression is legitimate, but the manager should say so rather than quietly drop 40 responses and report a theme count that no longer matches the responses.

whyWrong.A: Platform anonymity is about accounts and logins, not about whether the content can identify someone. Forty comments that name a project and a team are identifiable to the people involved.
whyWrong.C: The handling is defensible; the silence is not. A theme report that quietly excludes 40 responses misrepresents the data, and the survey owner may have views about the risk that prompted the exclusion.
whyWrong.D: Removing comments that name teams, projects or roles removes more than the 40 — it would strip a large share of an employee survey — and it still leaves content that identifies people without naming a team.

questions.mindset: Anonymity is a property of content, not of the platform — establish the risk with the survey owner and aggregate or suppress before use.

questions.scenario: A charity has a volunteer who wants to use Claude on their own account to help write an application for a grant worth £40,000. The charity has no AI policy. The application includes two references' names, the applicant's home address, and a detailed account of a disability that affects their eligibility.
questions.stem: What is the MOST appropriate response?

options.text: Support the use: no policy exists, the volunteer is acting in the charity's interest, and the grant is time-critical.

Do not support it. The absence of a policy is not a permission, the personal account is outside the charity's control, and the material includes health information about an identifiable applicant that has no place in a draft on an unmanaged account.
Support it provided the volunteer removes the references' names and the home address, since those are the clearly identifying items.
Support it but ask the volunteer to show the charity's trustee before submitting, so there is a record of the decision.

questions.explanation: Three things stack up. There is **no policy**, and silence is not permission. It is a **personal account**, so the charity cannot govern, audit or clean up what is written into it. And the material includes a **named applicant's health information** connected to an eligibility decision. Time pressure and good intent do not change any of those, and 'the trustee saw it afterwards' is not a control — the data has already been written into an account outside the charity.

whyWrong.A: Each clause is a reason for caution rather than for comfort. Absence of policy, an ungoverned account and special-category data about an identifiable person are the substance of the problem, not incidental.
whyWrong.C: Removing the two most obvious identifiers leaves the disability account, which attaches to one identifiable applicant in a small applicant pool. It also leaves the whole document sitting in the personal account.
whyWrong.D: Showing the trustee afterwards cannot govern or retract what has already been written. A control has to be in place before the data goes into the system, not after.

questions.mindset: No policy is not permission, and a personal account cannot carry the charity's health information about an identifiable person.

questions.scenario: An account manager at Fenmoor Group has been asked by a long-standing client to 'get something like the report your team produced last quarter, but with AI'. The client has not seen a report produced with the tool, has not been told how it is used, and has no written requirement of their own.
questions.stem: What is the BEST response?

options.text: Produce the report with Claude and disclose in a footnote that an AI tool assisted with drafting.

Treat it as an open question, not a preference: ask the client what they want the disclosure to look like, confirm the firm's policy position, and agree before producing anything. The client's own standard and the firm's policy may not be the same.
Produce it with Claude without mentioning the tool, since the client's request implies consent and disclosure would be over-sharing.
Decline and deliver the previous format, since the client has no AI policy of their own.

questions.explanation: The client's request is not a policy, and the firm's is not the client's. A vague 'something like yours but with AI' leaves two things genuinely open: **what the client expects to be told**, and whether the firm's rules permit this for this kind of deliverable. Asking before producing anything is cheap; producing first and disclosing afterwards means the client learns about the change on your schedule rather than theirs. The other paths each substitute an assumption for the answer.

whyWrong.A: A footnote disclosure chosen unilaterally is not agreement. If the client's own standard or their sector's rules require more — a named methodology note, an assurance statement, or disclosure they must make themselves — a footnote can be insufficient and can look like an afterthought.
whyWrong.C: A client's request for output is not consent to the method, and 'over-sharing' is a poor basis for withholding how the work was produced. Consent to a deliverable and knowledge of its production method are different things.
whyWrong.D: The absence of a client-side policy is a reason to ask, not a reason to refuse. Refusing on this basis treats an unanswered question as a prohibition.

questions.mindset: When a client asks for AI-assisted work without stating their standard, the disclosure format is an open question to settle before producing anything.

questions.scenario: A fundraising officer's team uses Claude to draft thank-you letters to donors. A donor who has received four such letters asks directly whether a computer wrote them. The officer has not asked the donors' consent, has never disclosed the practice, and her company has no AI policy.
questions.stem: What is the MOST defensible response?

options.text: Tell the donor the truth, including that the letters were drafted with AI and reviewed by a member of staff, and treat the question as the trigger for setting a practice and telling existing supporters.
Answer carefully without confirming, on the basis that a donor who asks has not been told and might prefer not to know.
Apologise for the error, stop using the tool immediately and delete all drafts, so nothing further is built on the practice.
Point out that every letter was checked and approved by a person, which is the disclosure the donor is entitled to.

questions.explanation: Answering the direct question honestly is the only defensible route, and it is also the moment to **establish a practice rather than improvise one per letter**. A person having reviewed the letter is true and relevant to quality, but it is a different fact from how it was drafted, and a donor who asked that question is asking about the second. Leaving the practice unsettled means the next conversation is another improvisation.

whyWrong.B: Weaseling around a direct question from someone the organisation has corresponded with repeatedly damages the relationship more than the fact would, and it leaves the practice exactly as unsettled as it was.
whyWrong.C: Stopping and deleting treats an unanswered question as a violation. Nothing in the situation suggests the drafting was unacceptable — the gap is disclosure and consent, which deletion does not address.
whyWrong.D: Human review is a genuine part of the answer but not the answer to the question asked. Offering the quality control in place of the method is evasion, and a donor who was told only that will reasonably feel misled.

questions.mindset: When someone asks directly how the work was produced, tell them — then settle the practice so the next answer is not improvised.

questions.scenario: A policy at a law firm states: 'Documents prepared with AI assistance must be reviewed by a qualified lawyer before being sent to a party or the court.' A trainee has prepared a first draft of an agreed statement of costs using Claude, has checked it against the bill, and wants to send it to the other side today.
questions.stem: What is the correct position?

options.text: The trainee's own check against the bill satisfies the policy, since the trainee is a qualified person doing the review.
It does not satisfy the policy. A trained lawyer must review and approve it before it goes to the other side, and that is the review the policy requires.
It satisfies the policy as long as the trainee discloses in the covering email that the statement was drafted with AI.
It satisfies the policy provided the trainee is confident in every figure, since the substance has already been verified.

questions.explanation: The policy is about **who reviews**, and the substance being correct does not change who did the checking. A trainee verifying against the bill is good practice and worth saying so, but it is not the qualified-lawyer review the policy names, and this is a document going to another party. Disclosure in the covering email is a separate question from the firm's own internal control.

whyWrong.A: This misreads the policy by substituting the reviewer's seniority for the reviewer's competence in the relevant sense. If the trainee were a qualified lawyer, the point would be different; the policy names qualification because the risk is a legal document.
whyWrong.C: Disclosure and review are independent requirements. Telling the other side how it was drafted does not substitute for the firm's own control over what it sends.
whyWrong.D: Confidence is not a defined standard and does not satisfy a named requirement. The policy's condition is a review by a qualified lawyer, whatever the drafter's certainty.

questions.mindset: When a policy names who must review, checking the substance yourself does not satisfy it — the review it requires is specific.

questions.scenario: A senior manager at Halcyon Legal tells an assistant: 'The client's engagement letter says nothing about AI, but nobody will ever know, and the deadline is Friday. Just get it done and don't write it in the file.' The assistant believes using the tool is reasonable but is uneasy about omitting it from the file.
questions.stem: What is the BEST course of action for the assistant?

options.text: Follow the instruction, since the manager is senior, the deadline is real and the tool itself is not prohibited for this kind of work.

Use the tool where the firm's policy permits, record its use in the file as required, and raise the tension between a policy requiring disclosure and a manager asking for it to be omitted — with the manager or the firm's AI owner — rather than resolving it silently.
Decline the whole task rather than accept either the omission or the disclosure, since the disagreement makes the work unsafe to do.
Use the tool and disclose it in the file anyway, on the basis that the firm's policy outranks one manager's instruction.

questions.explanation: This is a **conflict between a policy and an instruction to act against it**, and the assistant's job is to surface it rather than resolve it unilaterally in either direction. Do the work the policy allows, record what the policy requires recorded, and put the disagreement in front of the person who can settle it. What must not happen is a quiet decision either way — in either direction it leaves the firm's records and its people with a different account of what happened.

whyWrong.A: Seniority and deadline pressure are exactly the conditions under which a policy gets quietly set aside, and the instruction is to remove the record of a tool's use rather than to omit a minor detail. The assistant becomes accountable for the gap.
whyWrong.C: Declining everything is not the alternative to this dilemma. The tool may well be permitted for parts of the task, and abandoning the whole engagement over one disputed instruction leaves the deadline unmet for no governance benefit.
whyWrong.D: This inverts the problem: the assistant is not the right authority to decide that policy outranks a manager. Disclosing over the manager's objection without escalating is as much a unilateral resolution as omitting.

questions.mindset: When asked to act against a policy, do what the policy allows, keep the record the policy requires, and escalate the conflict rather than settling it quietly.

questions.scenario: A colleague at Northgate Logistics asks a marketing assistant to do something she knows the AI policy forbids: take 200 customer contact records from the CRM and paste them into her own Claude account to find a mailing segment, because the policy only permits uploading customer lists to the company Enterprise workspace.
questions.stem: Which TWO responses are MOST appropriate? Choose TWO.

options.text: Decline the specific request, say why, and point her to the company workspace as the route the policy requires.
Ask her to strip names and email addresses first and then do it in her personal account, since de-identified records are not customer contact records.
Offer to do the segmentation with her in the company workspace, or to help her find a colleague who can, so the work still gets done.
Do it for her in the personal account without recording that you did, on the grounds that it is her data and her decision.

questions.explanation: The helpful response has two halves: **hold the boundary clearly** — declining the request and naming the policy, not the mood — and **keep the work alive** through the route the policy actually permits. Offering to do the segmentation properly means the assistant is being useful rather than obstructive. Note what the two rejected options share: each relocates the data outside the controlled system while pretending the substance is unchanged.

whyWrong.B: Removing names and addresses does not change which account the data lands in, which is the specific thing the policy governs. It also leaves a contact list that can be re-identified from other fields, and it was she who chose the personal account.
whyWrong.D: This accepts the request and adds a second problem — a hidden record. Doing the work on a personal account is the breach, and concealing it removes any chance of it being corrected.

questions.mindset: Decline the prohibited route by name, then offer the permitted one — never relocate the data and pretend the substance is unchanged.

questions.scenario: An insurance company has issued an AI policy naming a Head of Compliance as its owner. Over four months, staff have asked that owner about eleven separate questions, mostly 'is this one small thing allowed'. She answers each one privately and has told colleagues she finds the volume unmanageable. Two staff members have since used the tool on data outside the policy without asking.
questions.stem: What does this suggest the owner should change?

options.text: Answer future questions faster, so that asking becomes cheaper than not asking.

Move from private one-off rulings to published guidance: a short, written set of worked examples covering the common cases, plus a clear route for anything genuinely new. The volume and the two unasked cases both point to the same gap.
Require that any use of the tool be approved in advance by the policy owner, with no exceptions, until the volume reduces.
Tell staff the policy is guidance rather than rules, since the owner cannot enforce it as written.

questions.explanation: The pattern — eleven private questions, then two cases where nobody asked at all — is a **governance design problem, not a workload problem**. Private rulings do not scale and produce no record others can rely on, so the questions that never arrive are the ones nobody needed to feel safe about. Published worked examples turn the owner's existing eleven answers into a reusable standard, and a named route for genuinely new cases keeps the boundary clear without a queue.

whyWrong.A: Speed reduces the queue but leaves the structure unchanged. Staff still cannot see the reasoning in advance, so the two cases that skipped asking would probably still skip asking.
whyWrong.C: Prior approval on every use stops all the small legitimate work and will be bypassed rather than obeyed, which is exactly how the current informal pattern arose in the first place.
whyWrong.D: Relabelling the policy as non-binding removes the only reference point people have. The difficulty is that the guidance is unwritten, not that it is too strict.

questions.mindset: A stream of private rulings and a handful of unasked cases point to one gap — published guidance with a route for what it does not cover.

questions.scenario: A local authority's housing team used Claude to summarise 2,400 comments on a proposed development and produce a theme report for the planning committee. Several councillors who read the report have quoted it in public meetings as though it were the council's own consultation finding.
questions.stem: What is the MOST responsible interpretation?

options.text: The problem is only that the report's findings are presented without qualification, so the fix is to check the theme analysis carefully before the next committee meeting.

The problem is that the committee cannot tell what was summarising the comments and what the council concluded. A tool-generated summary of public comments is an input to the council's decision, not the council's finding, and the distinction needs to be visible in how the material is presented and minuted.
The problem is that councillors quoted the report without reading the underlying comments, which is an engagement issue rather than an AI issue.
The problem is that a summary cannot represent 2,400 comments faithfully, so consultation findings must be compiled by hand.

questions.explanation: The harm here is **attribution**, not accuracy. A summary of what 2,400 people said is a legitimate analytical input; what has gone wrong is that a machine-generated summary has been circulated and quoted as though it were the council's own conclusion. The responsibility is to make the provenance visible — in the report, in how it is presented, and in the minutes — so that a quoted sentence cannot be detached from what produced it.

whyWrong.A: Checking the analysis more carefully addresses a possible accuracy problem and does nothing about the misattribution, which is the actual issue. The report could be perfectly accurate and still be quoted as a council finding.
whyWrong.C: Whether councillors read the comments is a separate and interesting question. It does not change the fact that a summary was presented in a way that let it be mistaken for an official finding.
whyWrong.D: Summarising a large volume of consultation comments is a well-suited task, and hand compilation does not guarantee faithfulness either — it guarantees a different kind of incompleteness.

questions.mindset: The risk in a tool-generated summary of public input is attribution — make clear it is an input to the decision, not the decision.

questions.scenario: A publisher's marketing team has used Claude to produce the first drafts of 80 book descriptions. Two readers have since complained that descriptions contained claims about the authors' backgrounds. The descriptions were published.
questions.stem: What is the MOST appropriate response?

options.text: Correct the two descriptions, note the error with the marketing team and add a pre-publication check that biographical claims are verified against the author's own records.
Add a general instruction to the team's prompting telling it to avoid biographical claims, and continue without reviewing the 78 descriptions already published.

Consider whether any published claim about a real, identifiable person could be defamatory or distressing, and take advice on those cases specifically, as well as correcting the two that prompted complaints.
Treat this as a rare edge case, since two complaints out of 80 descriptions is a small proportion.

questions.explanation: Claims about **real, identifiable people** carry consequences that claims about a product do not, and the ones a reader has not complained about may simply have gone unnoticed. The proportionate response is to consider the category of harm — defamatory or distressing statements about identified individuals — and get advice on those cases, rather than treating a complaint count as the measure. A verification step is the durable fix, but it addresses the future, not the material already published.

whyWrong.A: Correcting two descriptions is necessary and not sufficient. It addresses the complaints that arrived, and leaves the same claims standing in the other 78 where nobody happened to notice.
whyWrong.B: A general instruction reduces the chance of recurrence and leaves 78 published descriptions containing unverified claims about real people. It also treats the symptom rather than the class of harm.
whyWrong.D: A proportion is the wrong measure when the harm falls on named individuals. The two who complained are the ones who were noticed to be affected, not a bound on how many were.

questions.mindset: Claims about real identifiable people need a harm check across what was published, not a fix limited to what was complained about.

questions.scenario: A charity's fundraising team has used Claude for two years to draft appeals, impact summaries and thank-you letters. Their internal guideline, written at the start, says 'AI may be used for drafting; a named member of staff must approve anything published'. Nine months ago a trustee joined who had no view on AI use at all, and last month that trustee's view was added to the guideline: 'I would prefer we did not use it.'
questions.stem: What is the BEST way for the team to proceed?

options.text: Stop using the tool entirely, because a trustee's preference is now part of the guideline.

Take the trustee's preference to the board as a decision for the body's named owner, because one member's view in a guideline written for approval rules is not the same as the organisation's decision.
Continue exactly as before, since a view recorded in a guideline is advisory and the existing approval rule is unchanged.
Ask each member of staff to decide individually whether to use the tool, so that individual preference is respected without a policy decision.

questions.explanation: A guideline that names an approval step is a document where **decisions belong to a named owner**, and a preference added by one trustee has been recorded there without that route. It is a real input — the trustee's view should not be dismissed as unimportant — but it is not a decision, and quietly reverting to prior practice or quietly abandoning the tool both avoid the question. Taking it to the body's named owner is the step that settles it properly.

whyWrong.A: This treats one member's recorded view as the organisation's decision, in a document whose own design says decisions come through the named owner. It also discards two years of established practice on the strength of an informal addition.
whyWrong.C: Ignoring a documented preference inside your own guideline leaves the team in exactly the ambiguity the guideline exists to remove, and it puts the individual users in the position of deciding.
whyWrong.D: Handing the decision to individuals fragments the practice, makes the output inconsistent, and leaves nobody accountable for whether the organisation's stated policy is being followed.

questions.mindset: A preference recorded in an approval document is an input to the named owner, not the decision itself.

questions.scenario: An organisation has hired Claude across 60 staff with no written AI policy. Six months in, a staff survey shows wide disagreement about what is allowed: one team uses it for everything, another treats any use as a breach of confidentiality, and three people have used it on data they later believed was out of bounds.
questions.stem: Which TWO actions would MOST improve the position? Choose TWO.

options.text: Establish a named owner for AI use and a written policy built from the organisation's actual work — what data may be used where, which uses need review, and how anything AI-assisted is marked.
Run a session on the risks of AI and tell staff to use their judgement, since a policy written by management would not reflect how the work is actually done.
Review the three cases where staff used data they now believe was out of bounds, decide what happens in each, and treat them as the evidence for where the policy needed to say more.
Ban AI use for anyone who has not completed training, and set the training to cover the tool's features.

questions.explanation: Wide disagreement plus three uncertain cases is the picture of a **missing standard**, and the standard is what makes the disagreement resolvable: a named owner, and written rules tied to the work people actually do. The three cases are the most valuable material available, because they show precisely where the gap was — they are the evidence for what the policy needed to say. A training course about features and a general appeal to judgement both leave the underlying absence in place.

whyWrong.B: Asking staff to exercise judgement is what has produced the disagreement. Risk awareness is worth having, but it cannot substitute for a statement of what is allowed, and 'a policy written by management would not reflect the work' describes a reason to consult, not a reason to avoid writing one.
whyWrong.D: Training gates who uses the tool but not what they put in it. The three uncertain cases were not caused by people who had not been trained on features.

questions.mindset: Disagreement plus a handful of uncertain cases means the standard is missing — write it, and use the cases as the evidence of what it must cover.

questions.scenario: A marketing team has run a weekly campaign report with Claude for eight months. A new analyst joins and asks how the figures in the last six reports were produced. She is told the report is 'prompted from the CRM export' and that the numbers come 'from the data', and she finds no documented method. She cannot tell whether a figure was read from the export or inferred.
questions.stem: What is the MOST responsible next step for the new analyst to take?

options.text: Ask the team to document how the reports are produced — what the source export is, which figures are read and which are computed or estimated, and what a reader is meant to rely on — and treat past reports as provisional until that is in place.
Independently re-derive this month's figures from the CRM export before using anything, and keep doing it every month going forward.
Do not use the reports for anything, and raise the absence of a documented method with the marketing director.
Assume the figures are reliable, since eight months of reports have been circulated without anyone disputing them.

questions.explanation: The problem is that nobody — including the people who read the reports — **knows which figures are sourced and which are inferred**, so nobody can say what a reader is entitled to rely on. Documenting that method is the durable fix and it is also what allows past reports to be assessed at all. Her own re-derivation is a reasonable check on one month but leaves the same gap open next month, and eight months of unchallenged circulation is an absence of evidence rather than evidence of accuracy.

whyWrong.B: Re-deriving this month is useful verification and does not address why the method is unknown. Next month she faces the same absence, and no one else has gained anything.
whyWrong.C: Declining to use the reports leaves six months of circulating work untouched and gives the team no route to fix it. The gap needs closing, not avoidance.
whyWrong.D: That reports have circulated unchallenged shows nobody has been checking, not that the figures are sound — which is consistent with the analyst's difficulty establishing what is read and what is inferred.

questions.mindset: When nobody can say which figures are sourced and which are inferred, document the method before relying on the output.

questions.scenario: A lender's mortgage team has used Claude to summarise income and employment documents for 18 months. A compliance review asks how a decision-support summary is produced and what the team does when the tool is uncertain. The team cannot describe either, and three files in the last quarter contain a figure nobody can locate in the source documents.
questions.stem: Which TWO responses would BEST address the review? Choose TWO.

options.text: Stop using the tool for anything that feeds a lending decision until the method is documented and the three unlocatable figures are traced.
Require that any figure not found in the source documents be marked as unverified rather than presented as fact, and trace the three cases in the last quarter.
Retrain the team on how to prompt the tool more accurately, on the basis that the three figures are a prompting problem.
Explain to the review that the tool is a summarisation aid only, that final decisions are made by underwriters, and that this is sufficient.

questions.explanation: Two things are wrong: a consequential use with **no documented method**, and figures presented as fact that cannot be traced to source. The proportionate response is to suspend the consequential use while both are addressed, and to adopt a rule that unlocatable figures are marked as unverified rather than stated flatly — which is what makes a lending decision able to tell sourced from inferred. Retraining on prompting does not create traceability, and 'a human decides at the end' is not an answer to 'how does this work'.

whyWrong.C: Prompting quality is worth improving and does not address the review's question. Three figures nobody can locate is a provenance failure, and a better prompt does not make a figure traceable to a document.
whyWrong.D: This restates the arrangement without answering it. Where the method is undocumented and untraceable figures have reached decisions, the fact that a person signs off is a statement of the process, not an account of how it works.

questions.mindset: Undocumented method plus untraceable figures in a consequential decision is two failures — suspend the consequential use and require sourced figures to be marked.
